summary: Eugene Yan's talk covers building blocks for LLM systems and products, focusing on five of seven key patterns: evaluations, RAG, guardrails, user feedback collection, and brief mentions of caching and defensive UX. Evals are the foundation—enabling eval-driven development and safe deployments. Challenges include lack of consistent metrics, prompt sensitivity in benchmarks like MMLU, outdated academic benchmarks, and task mismatch. Best practices include building task-specific evals starting small (e.g., 40 questions), simplifying tasks for deterministic checks, using LLM-as-judge cautiously for open-ended tasks, and eyeballing outputs. For RAG, Yan highlights the 'lost in the middle' phenomenon where document position affects accuracy (first position best, middle worse than no RAG, even perfect retrieval yields only 75% accuracy), and LLMs' reluctance to reject irrelevant context. He recommends borrowing from information retrieval and applying relevance thresholds. Guardrails address safety and factual consistency via NLI at sentence-level granularity, sampling consistency checks, and strong LLM evaluation, with simpler methods often outperforming expensive approaches. Collecting user feedback builds evals and fine-tuning datasets as transferable assets across model generations. Explicit feedback (thumbs up/down) is sparse—few users click even among beta testers. Implicit feedback is noisy—copying a code snippet doesn't mean it's correct. GitHub Copilot captures rich implicit feedback through accept/reject actions dozens of times daily. Midjourney encodes nuanced reward signals: rerunning is negative, varying (V) is small positive, upscaling (U) is large positive. Yan concludes with three key takeaways: automate evals starting with 30-100 examples, reuse existing systems like BM25 and two-stage retrieval, and recognize UX as a major factor in LLM product success and feedback collection.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Evaluations
sections.summary: Evals are the foundation of LLM systems, enabling eval-driven development and safe deployments. Challenges include lack of consistent metrics, prompt sensitivity in benchmarks like MMLU, outdated academic benchmarks, and task mismatch. Best practices: build task-specific evals starting small (e.g., 40 questions), simplify tasks for deterministic checks, use LLM-as-judge cautiously for open-ended tasks, and eyeball outputs.

sections.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
sections.summary: RAG adds external knowledge without fine-tuning but faces LLM-side challenges. The 'lost in the middle' experiment shows document position affects accuracy—middle positions worse than no RAG, and perfect top retrieval only yields 75%. LLMs also struggle to reject irrelevant context, as shown by the Twilight/Sci-Fi recommendation example. Solutions include borrowing from IR and applying relevance thresholds.

sections.title: Guardrails
sections.summary: Guardrails ensure safety (moderation APIs) and factual consistency. Three approaches from summarization: NLI at sentence-level granularity (finer is better), sampling consistency (divergent summaries suggest hallucination), and strong LLM evaluation. Simpler methods often outperform expensive LLM-based approaches at lower cost.

sections.title: Collecting User Feedback
sections.summary: Collecting feedback builds evals and fine-tuning datasets—transferable assets across model generations. Explicit feedback (thumbs up/down) is sparse; implicit feedback is noisy. GitHub Copilot captures rich implicit feedback through accept/reject actions dozens of times daily. Midjourney encodes reward signals: rerun = negative, vary = small positive, upscale = large positive. Design products to build implicit feedback data flywheels.

sections.title: Conclusion: Three Key Takeaways
sections.summary: Three things to remember: (1) Automate evals—start with 30-100 annotated examples; eyeballing doesn't scale and automated evals enable rapid iteration and safe deployment. (2) Reuse existing systems—BM25, metadata matching, and recommendation system techniques like two-stage retrieval and ranking are already optimized for relevance. (3) UX plays a large role in LLM products—GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT's UX makes LLMs accessible in-context, and good UX makes feedback collection far more effective.

demonstrations: Twilight vs. Sci-Fi movies: LLM asked if user would like Twilight given Sci-Fi preferences; instead of saying 'not applicable' per instructions, it recommended ET citing interspecies relationships, illustrating LLMs' difficulty rejecting irrelevant context

NLI for summarization: premise 'John likes all fruits' with hypothesis 'John likes apples' classified as entailment; 'John eats apples daily' as neutral; 'John dislikes apples' as contradiction—applied to document-summary pairs
NLI granularity ablation: checking factual consistency at document, paragraph, then sentence level shows accuracy of detecting inconsistency increases with finer granularity
ChatGPT thumbs up/down: audience poll shows very few users click feedback buttons even among beta testers, illustrating explicit feedback sparsity
Copy code button: clicking copy on a code snippet containing 'nrows is not a valid argument for pandas read_par' shows implicit feedback noise—copying doesn't equal correctness
GitHub Copilot feedback loop: accept/reject/move-on actions dozens of times daily create a golden dataset of implicit feedback

Midjourney reward signals: rerunning prompt = negative reward (user likes none), varying (V button) = small positive (potential but needs tweaks), upscaling (U button) = large positive (user likes it)
